entities.name: The Judaic Rabbinic Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Judaic Rabbinic Corpus comprises the foundational literature of Rabbinical Judaism produced between c. 200 BCE and 600 CE. At its core stands the Mishnah (c. 200 CE), the first major written compilation of Jewish oral traditions, codified by Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi. The Mishnah became the basis for the two Talmuds — the Jerusalem Talmud (Yerushalmi, c.

400 CE) and the monumental Babylonian Talmud (Bavli, c. 500 CE) — which together constitute the most authoritative body of Jewish law, ethics, philosophy, and narrative outside the Hebrew Bible itself. Midrash collections (Mekhilta, Sifra, Sifre, Genesis Rabbah) provide exegetical commentary on the Torah. This corpus transformed Judaism from a Temple-centered sacrificial religion into a portable, text-centered faith capable of surviving the destruction of the Second Temple and two millennia of diaspora.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Judaic Rabbinic Corpus shaped the trajectory of Judaism, influencing its development from a Temple-centered sacrificial religion to a portable, text-centered faith. Its foundational literature, particularly the Mishnah and Talmuds, remains the most authoritative body of Jewish law, ethics, philosophy, and narrative outside the Hebrew Bible.
